plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 13: Structure Determination: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a correlation chart mapping carbon-13 chemical shifts to functional-group environments, drawn as a stack of horizontal bars over a pale yellow gradient field. The horizontal axis is labeled "Chemical shift (delta)" and reads from 220 at the left down to 0 at the right, with labeled ticks every 20 units and the unit "ppm" printed past the zero; faint vertical gridlines rise from each tick. The vertical axis carries only the word "Intensity" beside a magenta arrow pointing up, so bar height records no measured quantity and simply keeps the ranges from overlapping. Each shaded gray bar spans the shift range where one kind of carbon absorbs and carries its label. From the bottom of the stack upward these read "C=O", stretching from 220 to about 160; "C=C", roughly 150 to 107; "Aromatic", just above it over a similar span; a short "C(triple bond)N" bar near 130 to 120; "C(triple bond)C" near 95 to 80; "C-O" near 88 to 68; "C-N" near 78 to 55; a long "C-Hal" bar reaching from about 80 down to 10; then "-CH-" near 60 to 42, "-CH2-" near 50 to 28, and "-CH3" near 30 to 18 at the top. Laying every bar against one shared shift scale lets the reader see that carbons bonded to oxygen, nitrogen, or halogen fall well to the left of ordinary alkane carbons, which is what makes the chart usable for assigning the resonances of an unknown.

interactionPlan.concept: 13C NMR assigns functional groups by the range of chemical shifts where each carbon environment absorbs, with more deshielded carbons (C=O, C–O, C–N, C–Hal) appearing farther left on the reversed 220→0 ppm scale.

interactions.label: Chemical shift cursor (ppm)
interactions.teaches: Dragging the cursor across the scale shows that a given δ value can fall inside several functional-group ranges at once — assignments come from overlapping ranges, not single exact values, and the side list of intersecting groups is exactly the candidate list a spectroscopist would consider

Each functional group occupies a characteristic ppm interval whose endpoints define the assignment window, and groups bonded to electronegative atoms sit farther left (more deshielded) on the reversed δ scale

demo_steps.title: The deshielded end
demo_steps.narration: With the cursor at 220 ppm, only the C=O bar lights up — carbonyl carbons are the most deshielded common environment and sit alone at the far left of the scale.

demo_steps.title: The overlap zone
demo_steps.narration: Move the cursor to about 130 ppm: now C=C, Aromatic, and C≡N all glow together. A peak here narrows the possibilities but cannot by itself pick one group — ranges overlap.

demo_steps.title: Electronegative neighbors
demo_steps.narration: Near 70 ppm the C−O, C−N, C−Hal, and C≡C ranges intersect. Hover any glowing bar to read its exact endpoints and see the shaded window it claims on the axis.

demo_steps.title: Ordinary alkane carbons
demo_steps.narration: Sweep to about 25 ppm: only −CH2− and −CH3 (and the long C−Hal tail) remain. Shielded alkane carbons cluster at the right-hand, upfield end of the scale.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A 13C chemical shift identifies a functional group only up to the set of ranges that contain it — electronegativity pushes absorption leftward (deshielded, toward 220 ppm), so position on the reversed δ scale, not a single number, carries the structural information.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Reversed horizontal axis: 220 on the left, 0 on the right, ticks every 20 ppm with faint full-height gridlines, 'ppm' label just past zero, axis title 'Chemical shift (δ)'. Vertical axis is decorative only: the word 'Intensity' beside a magenta upward arrow at far left, no tick marks. Background is a pale yellow gradient fading toward the bottom. Eleven flat gray horizontal bars stacked without overlapping heights, ordered bottom-to-top C=O, C=C, Aromatic, C≡N, C≡C, C−O, C−N, C−Hal, −CH−, −CH2−, −CH3; labels centered on each bar in serif text with proper bond notation (double/triple bonds). Slider drives a thin vertical cursor line across the chart; bars intersecting it gain a warm glow/highlight and their names list beside the chart. Hovering a bar shows its ppm endpoints as a small tooltip and lightly shades that span along the x-axis.

authoredContext:
At its simplest, 13C NMR makes it possible to count the number of different carbon atoms in a molecule. Look at the 13C NMR spectra of methyl acetate and 1-pentanol shown previously in the figureb and the figureb. In each case, a single sharp resonance line is observed for each different carbon atom.

Most 13C resonances are between 0 and 220 ppm downfield from the TMS reference line, with the exact chemical shift of each 13C resonance dependent on that carbon’s electronic environment within the molecule. The figure shows the correlation of chemical shift with environment.

The factors that determine chemical shifts are complex, but it’s possible to make some generalizations from the data in the figure. One trend is that a carbon atom’s chemical shift is affected by the electronegativity of nearby atoms. Carbons bonded to oxygen, nitrogen, or halogen absorb downfield (to the left) of typical alkane carbons. Because electronegative atoms attract electrons, they pull electrons away from neighboring carbon atoms, causing those carbons to be deshielded and to come into resonance at a lower field.

Strategy Identify the distinct carbons in the molecule, and note whether each is alkyl, vinylic, aromatic, or in a carbonyl group. Then predict where each absorbs, using the figure as necessary.

discrepancies: The x-axis title is padded with a long run of spaces ('Chemical shift (δ)      ppm') to force 'ppm' to the right edge — a fragile hack that can misplace the unit at different widths, whereas the source has 'ppm' cleanly right-aligned below the axis.
The C−Hal bar extends to ~80 ppm in the generated figure, noticeably wider than the source's roughly 10–65 ppm span.

The C≡C range in the source spans roughly 70–95 ppm while the generated bar is 80–95, and the source's 'Aromatic' bar sits slightly left (higher δ) of C=C rather than sharing an identical 110–150 span.

The source stair-steps bars from CH3 (top-right) down to C=O (bottom-left); the generated figure inverts the vertical order (C=O on top), which is recognizable but reverses the reading direction of the staircase.
evaluation.notes: A faithful and pedagogically strong re-creation: reversed ppm axis, tan range bars, cream background, and magenta Intensity arrow all match, and the cursor slider, candidate highlighting, hover shading, click popups, and 4-step narrative all work; minor range inaccuracies and the space-padded axis-title hack are the main blemishes.
action_items: Replace the space-padded x-axis title with a proper right-aligned 'ppm' element (e.g. drawn in the deco plugin or a second title) so the unit stays anchored at any viewport width.
Correct the bar ranges to match the source: C−Hal ≈10–65, C≡C ≈70–95, and offset Aromatic slightly downfield of C=C.
Consider matching the source's vertical order (CH3 at top, C=O at bottom) to preserve the original staircase reading direction.
